explanations.explanation: Nahum says the opposite, friend. Verse 3 opens, “The LORD is slow to anger and great in power…” So the avenging God of verse 2 is also the slow-to-anger God. Quick to anger is the driver who honks at a green light half a second after it turns, and that is not how Nahum describes the LORD.

Right, and Nahum says it plainly: “The LORD is slow to anger and great in power…” That sits in the same breath as the avenging and the wrath. Slow to anger is a very different thing from quick to anger. A quick-tempered person has hair-trigger anger, and that isn't the picture Nahum paints.

That's it. Right after calling Him slow to anger, Nahum says, “…the LORD will by no means leave the guilty unpunished.” Slow to anger doesn't mean the guilty get a pass. Both things are true of Him at the same time.

explanations.answer: He will forget them over time
explanations.explanation: Nahum never hands time that job. Time smooths a lot of things over, like a burnt thumb from a hot cookie tray. But the verse says, “…the LORD will by no means leave the guilty unpunished.” Nothing in it says the guilty get lost in the shuffle.

explanations.answer: He will let them all go free
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what the verse says. Nahum says, “…the LORD will by no means leave the guilty unpunished.” "By no means" is about as strong as a phrase gets. So no, nobody walks out the side door.

Yes, it wilts. Verse 4 says, “Bashan and Carmel wither, and the flower of Lebanon wilts.” Bashan and Carmel are places, and they wither right along with it. When the LORD rebukes the sea and the rivers, the land feels it too.

I wish my cookie decorations did that, but no. Nahum says, “Bashan and Carmel wither, and the flower of Lebanon wilts.” Bashan and Carmel are places, and the whole scene is one of things drying out. The flower of Lebanon wilts right along with the rest.
Not in this verse, friend. Nahum says, “Bashan and Carmel wither, and the flower of Lebanon wilts.” Nothing in that line stays fresh. Everything droops when the sea and the rivers run dry.

That's the one. Nahum says, “The mountains quake before Him, and the hills melt away…” Mountains are the biggest, steadiest things around, and they shake when the LORD is there. If they quake, I'd be shaking in my apron.

Mountains are known for standing still, so I get the guess. But Nahum says, “The mountains quake before Him, and the hills melt away…” The biggest things around are the ones that shake. Nobody here is standing calmly.
Not in this verse, baker. Nahum says, “The mountains quake before Him, and the hills melt away…” It's a scene of shaking, with the earth trembling at His presence. There's no singing in this one.

It's true. Verse 6 says, “His wrath is poured out like fire; even rocks are shattered before Him.” Rocks are about the toughest thing you can name. When even they shatter, that tells you how great His power is, friend.

This one is actually true, baker. Nahum says, “His wrath is poured out like fire; even rocks are shattered before Him.” Rocks are about as tough as it gets, and they still don't hold up. That's the point of the line.

Yes. Verse 7 says, “The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of distress; He cares for those who trust in Him.” Right after the storm and fire, Nahum puts the focus on trust. That's a lot of comfort packed into one line, friend.
Nahum never says that. He says, “He cares for those who trust in Him.” Strength isn't the thing He looks for in this verse. Trust is.
If that were the rule, I'd be out, friend. I've botched whole batches of cookies. Nahum says, “He cares for those who trust in Him.” The verse names trust, and it says nothing about a perfect record.
Nahum says the opposite. Verse 8 says the LORD will “pursue His enemies into darkness.” Pursue means He's going after them, not waving as they slip away. Nobody sneaks out the back in this verse.

Right. Nahum says He will “pursue His enemies into darkness.” Pursuing is the opposite of letting someone escape. It's like chasing a runaway cookie across the counter, except this is a lot more serious than a runaway cookie.

explanations.answer: It will not rise up a second time
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. Verse 9 says, “Affliction will not rise up a second time.” Whatever gets brought to an end doesn't come back for round two. It's a promise that the trouble won't repeat.

explanations.answer: It will come back twice as strong
explanations.explanation: Nahum says the opposite. Verse 9 says, “Affliction will not rise up a second time.” No sequel, no comeback tour. If it were coming back stronger, the verse would sound very different.

explanations.answer: It will last for many more years
explanations.explanation: That's not what Nahum says, friend. Verse 9 says, “Affliction will not rise up a second time.” The verse is about it not returning, not about it dragging on. It's a promise of an end.

Yes, dry. Nahum says they'll be consumed “like stubble that is fully dry.” The word is fully dry, not just a little dry. Think of a crumb that's been sitting out so long it crunches when you look at it.
Close in sound, but no. The verse says, “like stubble that is fully dry.” Soaked is the opposite of dry. A soggy cookie is a sad cookie, and stubble in this verse is the dry kind.
Green is a fine color for a lot of things, baker, but not this. Nahum says, “like stubble that is fully dry.” Dry is the word in the verse.

explanations.answer: They will be cut down and gone
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The LORD says, “Though they are allied and numerous, yet they will be cut down and pass away.” Allied and numerous sounds like a big crowd with backup. The LORD says it still won't matter.

explanations.answer: They will be spared this time
explanations.explanation: That's not what the LORD says here. He says, “Though they are allied and numerous, yet they will be cut down and pass away.” The "yet" in that line matters. Even with lots of friends, they don't get spared.
It sounds like they might, with all those allies. But the LORD says, “Though they are allied and numerous, yet they will be cut down and pass away.” Numerous doesn't save them. They pass away.

It's true, baker. The LORD says, “Though I have afflicted you, O Judah, I will afflict you no longer.” Judah is the kingdom that stayed with David's family (1 Kings 12:20). After Nineveh's bad news, this is a gentle turn for Judah.

This one is actually true. The LORD says, “Though I have afflicted you, O Judah, I will afflict you no longer.” Judah is the kingdom that stayed with David's family (1 Kings 12:20). The words of comfort are right there in the verse.
That's it. The LORD says, “For I will now break their yoke from your neck and tear away your shackles.” Break the yoke and tear away the shackles. Those are both things coming off Judah.

Tightening is the opposite of what He says. The LORD says, “For I will now break their yoke from your neck and tear away your shackles.” He's taking things off, not putting more on. Judah gets relief here.

Locking up would be going the wrong way, friend. The LORD says, “For I will now break their yoke from your neck and tear away your shackles.” Shackles are already on Judah in this verse, and He's removing them. Nobody is getting locked up.
The command says the opposite. The LORD says, “There will be no descendants to carry on your name.” This part is heavy, friend. It's a serious word about Nineveh's end.
Yes. The LORD's command says, “There will be no descendants to carry on your name.” No one will carry Nineveh's name forward. It's a heavy word, and Nahum doesn't soften it.

That's what the LORD says. In verse 14 He says, “I will prepare your grave, for you are contemptible.” The LORD gives the reason right in the verse. It's a heavy line, and Nahum just states it plainly.
Not in this verse, baker. The LORD says, “I will prepare your grave, for you are contemptible.” Verse 14 gives no second chance. It's a heavy line, and it's about an ending.

The verse goes in a different direction. The LORD says He will cut off the carved image and cast idol from the house of Nineveh's gods. Then He says, “I will prepare your grave, for you are contemptible.” Nobody is building anything new here.
Yes. Nahum says, “Celebrate your feasts, O Judah; fulfill your vows.” With good news on the way, Judah is told to celebrate. That's one of my favorite lines in the whole chapter, friend.

The hills show up in the verse, but not for hiding. Nahum says, “Look to the mountains,” because the one bringing good news is coming from there. Then he says, “Celebrate your feasts, O Judah; fulfill your vows.” Judah is told to celebrate, not hide.
It's the other way around, baker. Nahum says, “Celebrate your feasts, O Judah; fulfill your vows.” The good news is about peace. So the call is to celebrate.

True. Nahum says, “For the wicked will never again march through you; they will be utterly cut off.” Never again is a big promise. That's good news for Judah, and it's the kind of line you'd tell a friend.

This one is true, friend. Nahum says, “For the wicked will never again march through you; they will be utterly cut off.” The key words are never again. Judah gets a promise that the wicked won't march through it again.
